'''Eric Boswell''' (born '''Eric Simpson''', 18 July 1921 – 29 November 2009) was an English composer of popular songs and folk music, most famous for writing the children's Christmas song "[[Little Donkey]]".

== Early life ==
Eric Boswell was born in [[Millfield, Tyne and Wear|Millfield]], [[Sunderland]], England, son of a tailor and a seamstress. He studied piano from age seven and later organ under Clifford Hartley,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.sunderlandecho.com/news/local/memories_of_our_dad_1_1137845|title=Clifford Hartley|website=Sunderlandecho.com|accessdate=13 July 2020|archive-date=7 March 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110307195518/http://www.sunderlandecho.com/news/local/memories_of_our_dad_1_1137845|url-status=dead}}</ref> organist of Bishopwearmouth Church (now [[Sunderland Minster]]). After degrees in Electrical Engineering from [[University of Sunderland|Sunderland Technical College]] and Physics from [[Birkbeck College|Birkbeck College, London]], Boswell joined [[Marconi Company|Marconi]] as a scientist working with radar before becoming a Physics lecturer. Meanwhile, he spent his leisure time writing serious piano music and light songs. A composition he entered the 1950 Brighton Music Festival won first prize and several of his classical works were performed at London's [[Wigmore Hall]] during the 1950s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.sunderlandecho.com/news/local/all-news/little-donkey-star-eric-dies-1-1080415|title=Sunderland Echo report of Eric Boswell's death|website=Sunderlandecho.com|accessdate=13 July 2020|archive-date=3 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303234732/http://www.sunderlandecho.com/news/local/all-news/little-donkey-star-eric-dies-1-1080415|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== "Little Donkey" and 1960s pop writer ==

In 1959, while hawking his more commercial songs to London's [[Denmark Street|Tin Pan Alley]] music publishers, Boswell encountered [[Gracie Fields]] at the music publisher [[Warner/Chappell Music|Chappell]], who she was visiting to seek a song to revive her career. Boswell offered her "[[Little Donkey]]", his telling of Mary and Joseph's journey to Bethlehem, and Fields' recording and another by [[The Beverley Sisters]], made the song the Christmas hit of 1959, being No. 1 in the then dominant UK Sheet Music Chart from mid November until New Year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.onlineweb.com/theones/1950_sheet.htm|title=The UK Number Ones : 1950s Sheet Music Sales|website=Onlineweb.com|accessdate=13 July 2020}}</ref> The song was a hit again at Christmas 1960 for [[Nina & Frederik]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.officialcharts.com/charts/singles-chart/19601208/7501/|title=Official Singles Chart Top 50 &#124; Official Charts Company|website=Officialcharts.com|accessdate=13 July 2020}}</ref>

By now Boswell had a publishing contract with Chappell, and wrote songs for them through the 1960s including [[Matt Monro]]'s "I'll Know Her" and [[Ricky Valance]]'s "Why Can't We". The latter (Valance's follow up to "[[Tell Laura I Love Her]]"<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/wales/music/sites/ricky-valance/pages/biography.shtml|title=BBC Wales - Music - Ricky Valance - Biography|website=Bbc.co.uk|accessdate=13 July 2020}}</ref>) came third in 1961's ''[[Eurovision: Your Country Needs You|A Song For Europe]]''. Boswell wrote the second placed song as well, "Suddenly I'm in Love", sung by Steve Arlen, which fell one vote short of representing the UK at 1961's [[Eurovision Song Contest 1961|Eurovision Song Contest]]. Meanwhile, "Little Donkey" was steadily re-recorded by artists as diverse as [[Vera Lynn]], [[Don Estelle]], [[St Winifred's School Choir]] and, in later decades, [[Aled Jones]], [[Patti Page]], [[Camera Obscura (band)|Camera Obscura]] (who performed the song as part of a [[John Peel|John Peel Session]]) and [[Cerys Matthews]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Artists who have recorded Little Donkey |url=http://www.last.fm/search/overview?q=little+donkey&type=track |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130724153843/http://www.last.fm/search/overview?q=little+donkey&type=track |url-status=dead |archive-date=2013-07-24 }}</ref>

In 1970, Boswell wrote another Christmas song "Boy From Bethlehem", for his new publishers William Elkin.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.elkinmusic.com/|title=Classical Sheet Music from Elkin Music International|website=Elkinmusic.com|accessdate=13 July 2020}}</ref> Although always in the shadow of "Little Donkey", "Boy From Bethlehem" was recorded by the London Children's Choir<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fcmg.org.uk/|title=Finchley Children's Music Group – London's Children's Choir|accessdate=13 July 2020}}</ref> and like its predecessor is often sung in British schools at Christmas.<ref>{{cite web|title=Mill Hill County High School|url=http://www.mhchs.org.uk/force_download.cfm?id=184|website=Mhchs.org.uk|access-date=24 July 2013|archive-date=20 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131220022648/http://www.mhchs.org.uk/force_download.cfm?id=184|url-status=dead}}</ref> As well as being a jobbing pop writer, Boswell was continuing to write classical library music and his ''The Enchantress'' has underscored several films.

Because Boswell had been concerned his academic employers would disapprove of his extracurricular career, he used a pen name derived from Boswell's Drive, [[Chelmsford]], the street where he lived. Eventually, just ahead of his 1976 remarriage, he also changed his real name by [[deed poll]] to Eric Boswell.

== The Geordie scene 1970s–1980s ==
By the end of the 1960s, following [[The Beatles]]' example, pop artists wrote their own songs rather than have backroom composers. Boswell instead began to write folk songs about his native [[North East Of England|North East England]], where he had returned to teach at [[University of Sunderland|Sunderland Polytechnic]]. A combination of local talent, generous arts funding and the patronage of regional ITV franchise [[ITV Tyne Tees|Tyne Tees]] meant the local cultural scene around [[Newcastle upon Tyne]] was thriving by the mid-1970s and Boswell, along with humorous dialect writer [[Scott Dobson]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.rolyveitch.20m.com/dialect_songwriters.html|title=WOR DIALECT - THE SONGWRITERS|website=Rolyveitch.20m.com|accessdate=13 July 2020}}</ref> and Geordie revivalist historian Joe Ging<ref>[http://www.rondrew.co.uk/theatre/Empire_Sunderland.htm]{{dead link|date=December 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> became key figures.

A Tyne Tees arts programme ''What Fettle'', presented by ''[[When The Boat Comes In]]'' actors [[Edward Wilson (actor)|Ed Wilson]] and [[James Bolam]], hired Boswell as musical director and his new songs and ballads about the North East featured weekly, performed by local soprano Marian Aitchison<ref>{{cite web|title=Marian Aitchison, Glendale Choir |url=http://www.durham.gov.uk/pages/providerdetails.aspx?ProviderId=47753 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131219020122/http://www.durham.gov.uk/pages/providerdetails.aspx?ProviderId=47753 |archivedate=19 December 2013 |df=dmy }}</ref> and tenors Ralph Hawkes and Michael Hunt, as well as in a networked programme ''Sounds of Britain''. Boswell's material (often described as '[[Geordie]]' but frequently set in the wider region including [[Northumberland]] and [[Wearside]]) was often very funny, sometimes ideological (including possibly the first song lamenting [[global warming]]), but always celebrated the peculiarities of the region, its self-deprecating humour and idiosyncratic [[Geordie dialect words|dialect]].

A local radio programme and later annual [[Newcastle City Hall]] show ''Geordierama'' was musically directed by Boswell and featured his songs alongside Northumbrian folk dancers, pipers and comedians. Hosted by local celebrities including [[Mike Neville (newsreader)|Mike Neville]], [[Bill Steel]] and [[Frank Wappat]], the stage ''Geordierama'' was part of the annual Newcastle Festival for much of the 1970s, later moving to the [[Mill Volvo Tyne Theatre|New Tyne Theatre]], and vinyl recordings of the shows were released. Meanwhile, Tyne Tees asked Boswell to write a song welcoming [[Jimmy Carter|President Jimmy Carter]] to the north on a [[American Bicentennial|1976 Bicentennial]] visit to his ancestral home in [[Washington, Tyne and Wear|Washington, Tyne & Wear]] which resulted in "Welcome To Geordieland". And in the early 1980s, [[Sunderland]] comedian [[Bobby Thompson (comedian)|The Little Waster, Bobby Thompson]] recorded several humorous songs written for him by Boswell.

Also in the 1980s Boswell, on piano, formed a chamber trio with Aitchison and Ging named Sounds of Tyne & Wear, which performed his songs around the region for many years, often called upon by the [[Lord Mayor]] of Newcastle to entertain visiting dignitaries to the city, which on one occasion included [[Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh|Prince Philip]].

== Musical theatre: Catherine Cookson's ''Katie Mulholland'' ==
[[File:Katie Mulholland Theatre Poster 1983.jpg|thumb|right|1983 poster promoting the stage musical ''Katie Mulholland'']]
In the early 1980s, Boswell approached Tyneside novelist [[Catherine Cookson]] with an idea (of his second wife, Lena) he adapt Cookson's semi-autobiographical ''Katie Mulholland'' into a stage musical. Directed by [[Ken Hill (playwright)|Ken Hill]], who also wrote dialogue around Boswell's songs, an elaborate staging formed the centrepiece of the 1983 Newcastle Festival, selling out [[Northern Stage, Newcastle upon Tyne|Newcastle Playhouse]] for five weeks. Boswell's slightly [[Stephen Sondheim|Sondheimesque]] score included pastiches of gospel, vaudeville and [[Barbershop quartet|barbershop]]. His existing song, "Jenny Was There", a paean to the annual funfair on [[Newcastle Town Moor]] known as '[[The Hoppings|The Hoppin's]]' was suitably amended to 'Katie' for the production, but the other numbers were newly written. The musical's success may have inspired the flurry of subsequent stage and television dramatisations of Cookson's novels.

== New collaborations ==
In 1985, Boswell left Sunderland for the [[North Tyne]] village of [[Humshaugh]], where he would spend the rest of his life. The heyday of the Geordie scene had passed but he continued to write invariably humorous songs: leeks, whippets and racing pigeons all featuring, as did the new [[Gateshead Millennium Bridge|Millennium Bridge]] and [[MetroCentre (shopping centre)|Gateshead MetroCentre]]. The [[Tyneside]] a cappella choir Spectrum performed and recorded Boswell's work and [[County Durham]] opera singer [[Graeme Danby]], principal bass of [[English National Opera]], became an enthusiastic supporter: most of Boswell's later songs being written for Danby and his partner, mezzo-soprano Valerie Reid, to perform at their Northumberland open-air concerts, and the pair released two albums of his material. Meanwhile, some of Boswell's 1970s ballads such as "Tyneside's Where I Come From", "Sweet Waters of Tyne" and "But It's Mine", had joined "[[Blaydon Races|The Blaydon Races]]" and "[[Lambton Worm|The Lambton Worm]]" in the canon of northern traditional songs, and are still regularly performed in the region's folk clubs.{{citation needed|date=January 2021}}

== Later life ==
Boswell was intensely private. He had mixed feelings about "Little Donkey",<ref>{{cite news|title=Eric Boswell Obituary|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/8390710.stm | work=BBC News | date=2 December 2009}}</ref> prouder of his humorous work, believing laughter was 'what life is all about'. In later years he rarely ventured beyond his beloved Northumberland countryside. He remained a celebrity in Humshaugh however, writing music for village shows and playing the church organ for services well into his eighties, often slipping in his own music or some [[Gilbert & Sullivan]] as the congregation left. In 2005, Boswell's record company MWM<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mawson-wareham.com/artists.php?artid=3&sename=Eric+Boswell|title=Eric Boswell - MWM Records - North East Music and Comedy|website=Mawson-wareham.com|accessdate=13 July 2020}}</ref> enhanced earlier analogue recordings to produce a retrospective double album of his folk songs. And early in 2009 Boswell attended a recording session for Graeme Danby's second album of his songs, which included a golden anniversary 'duet' of "Little Donkey" between Danby and Gracie Fields, some 30 years after the latter had died.<ref>{{cite web|title=Frank Wappat's Obituary of Eric Boswell|url=http://www.frankwappat.com/tributes-to-the-stars/53-eric-boswell-dies-at-88-.html|website=Frankwappat.com}}</ref>

Boswell married twice, Margaret (two sons and three grandsons) and Lena (one son), both his wives predeceased him. He died on 29 November 2009 aged 88, shortly after moving to a nursing home in [[Riding Mill]] and exactly 50 years after his most famous song was riding high in the UK chart.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.onlineweb.com/theories/1950+sheet.htm|title=UK Sheet Music Charts|website=Onlineweb.com|accessdate=13 July 2020}}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

== Eric Boswell Memorial Prize ==
An annual competition runs in Boswell's name for a new Folk song about the North East of England.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.dontmentionlittledonkey.com|title=Announcement of Eric Boswell Memorial Prize|website=Dontmentionlittledonkey.com|accessdate=13 July 2020}}</ref>

== Discography and bibliography ==
Eric Boswell: ''Left to Write'' (MWM Records, 1976), Spectrum: ''Spectrum Sing Boswell'' (1987), Graeme Danby & Valerie Reid: ''Take Me Up the Tyne'' (MWM Records), Various: ''Eric Boswell: Archive - Songs of the North'' (MWM Records, 2005), Graeme Danby & Valerie Reid: ''There's More to Life'' (MWM Records, 2009)

Eric Boswell: 'Little Donkey' (Chappell, 1959) – sheet music (and in many compilations), Eric Boswell: ''Boy from Bethlehem'' (William Elkin, 1970) – sheet music, Eric Boswell: ''Songs of the North East'' (in four volumes: North Tyne Publications, Vol 1–2, 1995, Vol 3–4, 2000) – piano/guitar songbooks, Jan Lewis: ''Little Donkey'' (Orchard, 2002) – children's picture book inspired by the song
